title: Drift detection
story:
Three different things drift, they produce the same symptom, and they need opposite responses. That is the whole difficulty, and a team that has not separated them spends its time arguing about which one it is without evidence either way.

The inputs drift: people start asking about things they did not ask about before, in different words, at different lengths, about a product feature that shipped last month. The corpus drifts: documents are edited, added and withdrawn, and the index built three months ago describes a world that has moved. And the model drifts: a provider updates what sits behind a name, and behaviour changes without any deploy of yours.

Each of those looks identical from where the complaints arrive. Quality has dropped. Each needs a different fix — new cases and possibly new content, a rebuilt index, a version comparison — and applying the wrong one wastes a week and leaves the problem in place.

So the first requirement is a baseline, because drift is a statement about a comparison. Numbers captured while things were working, stored durably, labelled with the versions in play. Without that fixed point, everything is a debate about whether it used to be better, and that debate cannot be settled by people who were not paying attention at the time.

Watch the inputs, because they are the cheapest thing to measure and the most neglected. The distribution of question lengths. The rate of terms that have never been seen before. Rough clusters of topic, however crudely computed. A sudden rise in unfamiliar vocabulary is a population telling you something changed on their side, and it usually precedes the complaints by a comfortable margin.

Watch the retrieval. How often it returns nothing, and the distribution of the best score it achieves. Both move when the corpus has changed underneath you or when the questions have moved away from what the corpus covers, and they move before the answers become visibly bad, because retrieval degrades gradually while answers stay fluent throughout.

Watch the outputs for the indicators that are not errors: refusal rate, output lengths, citation verification failures. And run the case set on a schedule, not only on a change, so that a drop caused by something outside your control still shows up somewhere.

Now the asymmetry that makes this lesson necessary, because it is the thing most teams get wrong. A fixed case set detects model drift and corpus drift and is blind to input drift by construction. If your users start asking a new kind of question, every case still passes, the dashboard stays green, and the system is failing the people using it. The set measures what you already knew to ask about, and drift in the inputs is precisely the arrival of what you did not.

That is why the input distribution is monitored separately and why sampled human review is not optional. Those two are the only instruments pointed outward at the world rather than inward at last quarter's expectations.

And when something does move, diagnose before you fix. Did the input distribution change? Then add cases and consider whether the content covers the new questions. Did retrieval health change while inputs stayed steady? Then look at the index and when it was last built. Did both stay steady while the case set dropped? Then compare model versions, because the thing that changed was not yours. The diagnosis takes an afternoon with the right instruments and is impossible without them.

problem.name: Telling three kinds of change apart
problem.shape: Quality has fallen and any of several independent things could have moved.
tell: answers are worse and nobody can say what changed
there are no recorded numbers from when things were working
the case set still passes while users are complaining
nothing is watching the distribution of incoming questions
problem.move: Capture a baseline while things work, then monitor the inputs, the retrieval health and the non-error output signals separately, run the case set on a schedule, and diagnose which of the three moved before changing anything.
problem.invariant: Drift is a comparison, so detecting it requires numbers recorded while the system was behaving, labelled with the versions that produced them.
problem.breaks: A fixed case set is blind to input drift by construction — if users start asking new kinds of question, every case still passes while the system fails the people using it.

cost.time: monitoring several distributions and running the set on a schedule rather than only on change
cost.space: baselines and windowed statistics have to be stored to be compared against
cost.beats: waiting for complaints, which arrive late and cannot distinguish causes, and re-running the case set alone, which cannot see the world moving

problem.practice: Count the terms in this week's questions that never appeared in any question from three months ago, then do the same for a week three months ago against six. If that rate is rising, your users have moved and your case set has not noticed, which is exactly the blind spot to fix first.

beats.broke: Inputs, corpus and model drift independently and produce the same complaint, so the wrong fix gets applied and the problem stays.
beats.fix: Capture a baseline while things work, monitor inputs, retrieval health and output indicators separately, and diagnose which one moved before changing anything.
beats.cost: Several distributions to monitor and store, and a fixed case set that cannot see input drift no matter how good it is.

interview.q: Three things can drift and they look the same from the outside — how do you tell which one moved?
interview.trap: Relying on the evaluation set to catch drift. It detects model and corpus change and is blind to input drift by construction, so it stays green exactly when users start asking something new.
